intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. The notes under each slide explain it, tell you what to remember and warn you where people slip. Work the examples in pencil before you read the steps, and answer the recall questions from memory.

sections.title: What Mixed Methods Is
sections.big_idea: Mixed methods is **integration by design**: two kinds of evidence combined so that a finding appears which neither strand could reach alone.
in_plain_words: Mixed methods research intentionally collects, analyses and integrates quantitative and qualitative data in one study. The operative word is integration. A survey and some interviews running in the same project are two studies in a trench coat until the strands inform each other or are merged and compared.

Development questions are naturally mixed. 'Did it work?' is quantitative, and 'for whom, why and how?' is qualitative. The promise is 1 + 1 = 3, and the caution is that mixing roughly doubles skills and time, and that two weak strands give one weak study. Mix because the question demands it.

left.title: Not yet mixed
items: A survey, and separately some interviews
Quotes added to illustrate a percentage

right.title: Mixed
items: Interviews chosen because of the survey
A finding neither strand reaches alone

diagram.caption: integration is the test, whatever the data types

key_terms.meaning: Intentional collection, analysis and integration of both kinds of data in one study.
The deliberate point where the quantitative and qualitative strands meet.
Two strands side by side, written up separately; the reader integrates.
The promise that integrated findings exceed the sum of the parts.
Two strands that never speak; Section 10's first pitfall.

worked_example.title: Apply the four-question test
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. A report has a survey chapter and an interview chapter. The interviewees were picked from survey results, the conclusions cite both strands, and the strands agree on everything.
steps: Did one strand influence the other's design? Yes: the sampling plan used the survey.
Is there a finding that needs both? Check the conclusions; the slide says to look there.
Was there a point where they met? Look for a joint display. None is mentioned.
Was divergence reported? Agreement on everything is suspicious and suggests nobody looked.
worked_example.answer: Partly mixed: connected by design, with no meeting point shown and no divergence reported.

mistakes: Calling a project mixed because it has a survey and interviews. The distinguishing feature is integration.
Adding interviews after the survey disappoints. That is a salvage operation and a weak design.
Mixing because it sounds rigorous in a proposal instead of because the question needs both.

recall.q: What is the operative word in the definition?
recall.a: Integration.

recall.q: What does the fourth question of the test ask?
recall.a: Whether divergence was reported, meaning whether any disagreement between the strands appears at all.

recall.q: Why is a null result uninterpretable alone?
recall.a: The theory could be wrong, or the programme could never have happened; implementation data separates them.

recall.q: Name two things mixing costs.
recall.a: More skills, time and coordination; it roughly doubles them.

recall.q: Which companion courses does this one pair with?
recall.a: Qualitative Methods and Data Literacy 101.

sections.title: Why Mix? Five Purposes
sections.big_idea: Greene's five purposes give mixing its vocabulary. **Name the purpose before the design**, because it decides what agreement between strands means.
in_plain_words: Triangulation seeks corroboration, complementarity layers depth on breadth, development has one strand build the other, initiation hunts for contradiction, and expansion widens scope by giving each strand a component. Each implies a design, and each says something different about agreement.

Only triangulation treats agreement as the test, and it needs the same construct, strong strands, independence and a real chance to disagree. In the other four, reporting that strands confirmed each other claims too much. Many good studies carry more than one purpose, so name each and say which strand serves it.

diagram.caption: the five purposes grouped by what they do

key_terms.meaning: Two methods on one phenomenon, seeking convergence.
Different facets of one issue, each elaborating the other.
One method's findings shape the next method.
Looking for contradiction that reframes the question.
Different methods for different components of the inquiry.

worked_example.title: Name the purpose
worked_example.setup: Five situations from the section. Give each its purpose.
steps: Survey shows immunisation rose; focus groups independently describe easier access. Triangulation.
Survey counts dropouts; interviews reveal menstruation, distance, safety. Complementarity.
Interviews generate the items for a survey instrument. Development.
Clinic satisfaction is high; interviews describe fury about waiting. Initiation.
A trial measures impact; a qualitative strand covers implementation. Expansion.

mistakes: Using the word triangulation for 'we did both'. The four conditions separate the claim from the thing.
Interviewing the same households right after surveying them with the same enumerator and calling it corroboration.
Treating expansion as if it integrated, when nothing forces its strands to meet.

recall.q: Who proposed the five purposes and when?
recall.a: Greene, Caracelli and Graham, in a 1989 review.

recall.q: Which purpose makes agreement meaningful?
recall.a: Triangulation.

recall.q: Which design does development imply?
recall.a: Sequential, in the order the building requires.

recall.q: Why leave slack in the timeline?
recall.a: So a contradiction found by initiation can be pursued instead of footnoted.

recall.q: What integration step does expansion need?
recall.a: A deliberate one, or it becomes parallel play.

sections.title: Paradigms & Pragmatism
sections.big_idea: Methods carry worldviews, and pragmatism answers the objection by letting **the question choose the method**. You must still notice where a disagreement comes from.
in_plain_words: A worldview is a shared set of beliefs about what reality is and how we can know it. Post-positivism and constructivism sit at opposite poles, and the incompatibility thesis argued that combining them is incoherent. The researcher's role is where most friction arises on mixed teams.

Pragmatism, associated with Tashakkori and Teddlie, replies that the research question matters more than the worldview. Other stances exist: dialectical, which holds the worldviews in tension, and equity-led, which starts from justice. All traditions share commitments to systematic procedures, checkable claims and findings that could be wrong.

diagram.caption: two poles, rarely held in pure form

key_terms.meaning: A set of beliefs about reality (ontology) and knowing (epistemology).
The claim that combining the two traditions is incoherent.
Choose methods by what answers the question.
Hold opposing worldviews in tension and use the friction.
Start from justice; design to shift power.

worked_example.title: Name the stance
worked_example.setup: Four colleagues each make a statement. Match it to a stance from the slide on stances.
steps: 'The paradigms are incompatible; do not mix.' That is the purist position.
'Choose by the question and set the dispute aside.' That is the pragmatist position.
'Hold both and use the tension productively.' That is the dialectical position.
'Start from justice and design to shift power.' That is the equity-led position.

mistakes: Describing a qualitative strand as 'indicative' or apologising for its sample, which applies a sampling logic it never claimed.
Taking pragmatism to mean method choice is arbitrary or truth is whatever is convenient.
Applying 'is it reliable?' to interviews or 'is it credible?' to a survey.

recall.q: What is the incompatibility thesis?
recall.a: The claim that quantitative and qualitative methods rest on irreconcilable worldviews.

recall.q: What does pragmatism ask first?
recall.a: What is the question, what would answer it, and what follows for action.

recall.q: What is the useful test of a pragmatist answer?
recall.a: Whether you can say what would count as being wrong.

recall.q: What do both traditions accept about sampling?
recall.a: Sampling decisions determine what can be said.

recall.q: What does 'mixing with eyes open' mean?
recall.a: Naming your stance, holding each strand to its own standard, and planning for disagreement.

sections.title: The Core Designs
sections.big_idea: Four designs cover most studies. **Capitals show priority, position shows order, the connector shows timing.**
in_plain_words: Notation from Morse and Creswell and Plano Clark writes a design in a line. Capital letters mark the dominant strand, lower case the supporting one, a plus means concurrent and an arrow means sequential. Two questions define every design: timing and priority.

Convergent parallel runs both at once, explanatory sequential follows the numbers with interviews, exploratory sequential builds an instrument from qualitative work, and embedded nests a supporting strand inside a larger design. Each has a scheduling failure. Real programmes chain them into multiphase designs, which multiplies integration points.

diagram.caption: timing and priority define each design

key_terms.meaning: Capitals mark the dominant strand, lower case the supporting one.
Both strands at once, merged and compared.
Quant first; qualitative follow-up explains.
Qual first; builds an instrument or typology.
A supportive strand nested in a dominant design.
Several designs chained over years.

worked_example.title: Read four notations
worked_example.setup: Use the three marks: capitals for priority, position for order, connector for timing.
steps: QUAL → QUAN: qualitative first, both weighted equally, for example build a scale then validate it.
quan → QUAL: a small survey to select cases, then the main qualitative study.
QUAN(qual): a trial with an embedded process evaluation.
QUAL + quan: an ethnography with a supporting descriptive survey.
worked_example.answer: Sequential equal weight, survey as sampling tool, embedded process strand, and concurrent qual-led.

mistakes: Describing a short sampling survey as a findings source, which overstates what it was built for.
Letting phase one run long so phase two shrinks to a few rushed calls.
Treating the embedded strand as decoration instead of giving it its own question.

recall.q: What are the two questions that define every design?
recall.a: Timing and priority.

recall.q: Which design is the most common in evaluation?
recall.a: Explanatory sequential.

recall.q: Where does a convergent design usually fail?
recall.a: At the join, with no real integration at the end.

recall.q: What purpose does exploratory sequential match?
recall.a: Development.

recall.q: What does QUAN(qual) mean?
recall.a: A qualitative strand embedded inside a dominant quantitative design.

sections.title: Choosing a Design
sections.big_idea: The question chooses the design. **Decide order, priority and point of contact**, then write the design down before fieldwork.
in_plain_words: Begin with what you need to know and ask three things: which strand leads or whether they run alongside, which carries more weight, and where they will meet. Timing is often forced by the calendar, and if so the methods should say so. Priority is set by resourcing whether or not anyone decides it.

Constraints rule designs out: a six-month timeline rules out a real phase two, and one researcher rules out concurrent strands. Match ambition to capacity. Then pin the design in the protocol with six lines: purpose, notation, priority, interface points, who integrates and when, and what happens if the strands diverge.

nodes.label: Question
nodes.sub: what do I need to know

key_terms.meaning: Both strands at once; faster, but they cannot shape each other.
One finishes before the next; A shapes B.
Which strand carries the main analytic load.
Where numbers and words connect: design, data, analysis or interpretation.
A one-line protocol entry in notation.

worked_example.title: Pick a design from a question
worked_example.setup: Use the question table on the slide Start Here, then check one constraint.
steps: 'Did it work, and why?' points to QUAN → qual.
'Do these two sources agree?' points to QUAN + QUAL, since independence requires simultaneity.
'What do people here think a good outcome is?' may need QUAL alone.
A six-month timeline rules out a sequential design with a real phase two, so choose a smaller design done properly.
worked_example.answer: QUAN → qual, QUAN + QUAL, QUAL alone; and shrink the design if time is short.

mistakes: Choosing 'explanatory sequential' because it is familiar and working out its purpose afterwards.
Declaring equal priority with most of the budget on one strand.
Treating 'integrated at analysis' as a plan without naming a display, a person or a week.

recall.q: What does concurrent timing prevent?
recall.a: The strands informing each other's design.

recall.q: What is priority signalled by in resourcing?
recall.a: Budget and time, which often override stated intent.

recall.q: Which interface point must be planned at the start?
recall.a: Linked identifiers at data collection.

recall.q: Name three of the six lines in the protocol.
recall.a: For example purpose, notation, priority and why, interface points, who integrates, divergence plan.

recall.q: What is the commonest planning error?
recall.a: Choosing a design you cannot resource.

sections.title: Sampling in Mixed Methods
sections.big_idea: Quantitative sampling represents and qualitative sampling illuminates. **Say how the two samples relate** and judge each by its own standard.
in_plain_words: Quant sampling is probability-based and sized by precision; qual sampling is purposive and sized by saturation. Mixed designs must hold both. Concurrent sampling keeps samples independent; sequential sampling draws the second from the first, and nesting links a person's numbers to their words.

Nesting needs a retained identifier, consent for recontact and secure contact details, and case-selection criteria written in advance. Choose cases on purpose: extreme, typical, deviant, maximum variation, confirming. Compare the frames, including dates, and record who you could not reach.

key_terms.meaning: Cases chosen for what they can show.
The point where new interviews stop yielding new themes.
One strand's sample drawn as a subset of the other's.
A case the quantitative model predicted badly.
Different units, populations, seasons or boundaries across strands.

worked_example.title: Write a case-selection rule
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. A survey of 1,200 households retained identifiers and consent to recontact. You want to find what the model missed.
steps: Fit the model and compute each household's residual.
Choose deviant cases: the twenty households with the largest residuals.
Write that rule in the methods before looking at which cases make a good story.
Check contact details are stored securely, because recontact is a data-protection matter.
worked_example.answer: 'Deviant cases, the twenty households with the largest residuals', stated in advance.

mistakes: Randomly picking interviewees from the survey sample and getting a representative dozen with nothing informative to say.
Running the survey in one season and the interviews in another, then explaining the false divergence.
Judging a qualitative sample by representativeness.

recall.q: What drives survey size?
recall.a: The precision needed for the smallest subgroup you will report.

recall.q: What drives interview size?
recall.a: Saturation.

recall.q: What two things does nesting need beyond a sample?
recall.a: A retained identifier and consent covering recontact.

recall.q: Why state selection criteria in advance?
recall.a: To avoid choosing cases that confirm what you already believe.

recall.q: What does the equity lens add to sampling?
recall.a: Deliberately over-listening to those the averages bury, such as Dalit, Adivasi, disabled and migrant respondents.

sections.title: Integration: the Heart
sections.big_idea: Integration is what makes a study mixed. **Build a joint display**, report convergence and divergence, and write the meta-inference as a deliverable.
in_plain_words: Integration is the deliberate point where strands are connected, merged or embedded. It matters most and gets scheduled least, because it produces no deliverable of its own. The tools are a joint display, following a thread across both datasets, and data transformation by quantitising or qualitising.

When strands agree, convergence is only as strong as their independence. When they clash, divergence is a finding to investigate and never a failure. The product is the meta-inference, a conclusion neither strand could reach alone. If your conclusions could be written from one strand, the integration has not happened.

diagram.caption: following a thread to a conclusion

key_terms.meaning: A table or figure arraying both strands around one principle.
Bringing both datasets together to compare them.
Turning qualitative codes into counts.
Turning quantitative profiles into narrative typologies.
Both strands pointing the same way.
A conclusion drawn across both strands.

worked_example.title: A theme count and its caveat
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. Twenty purposively selected interviewees were coded for the theme 'the fee'; twelve mentioned it.
steps: Count: 12 of 20 interviewees mentioned the fee.
Warn the reader: this is a count within a purposive sample and not a prevalence estimate.
The eight who did not mention it were never asked directly, so do not read 60% as a rate.
worked_example.answer: 60% of the twenty, reported as a count and not as an estimate.

mistakes: Filling the strand columns of a joint display and leaving the last column restating them.
Presenting a theme count as a prevalence estimate.
Footnoting divergence, which is the finding most likely to be right and least likely to be published.

recall.q: What is the removal test for integration?
recall.a: Remove either strand; if the conclusions barely change, you never integrated.

recall.q: Which way of integrating is hardest?
recall.a: Merging.

recall.q: Why is the satisfaction case a divergence?
recall.a: Surveys record high satisfaction while interviews record sustained complaint, often because of social desirability.

recall.q: What are the five reasons to check when strands clash?
recall.a: Different things measured, different populations or periods, social desirability, one strand wrong, both right.

recall.q: Where should the meta-inference appear?
recall.a: As its own labelled subsection.

sections.title: Quality & Validity
sections.big_idea: A mixed study faces **three quality bars**: the quantitative strand, the qualitative strand and the mixing itself. The third decides whether it was mixed.
in_plain_words: Hold each strand to its own standard. Quantitative work asks about representativeness, validity, generalisation and reproducibility. Qualitative work asks about case choice, credibility, transferability and an audit trail. Imposing one set of criteria on the other strand is a category error.

Legitimation is the standard specific to mixing: were the samples compatible, did integration happen, were meta-inferences warranted, was divergence handled. Quality also splits into design quality and interpretive rigour, which fail independently. Pre-specify, build a joint display and report the mixing as well as the methods.

diagram.caption: three bars, the third unique to mixed work

key_terms.meaning: Validity framework for mixing: are the meta-inferences defensible?
The qualitative counterpart of internal validity.
Enough context for the reader to judge applicability.
Record from data to claim: codes, coders, resolved disagreements.
Suitable, adequate and faithfully implemented design.
Meta-inferences that follow from the evidence.

worked_example.title: Match the quality terms
worked_example.setup: Use the table on the slide Each Strand. Match each quantitative term with its qualitative parallel.
steps: Internal validity pairs with credibility (truth value).
External validity pairs with transferability (applicability).
Reliability pairs with dependability (consistency).
Objectivity pairs with confirmability (neutrality).
worked_example.answer: Credibility, transferability, dependability, confirmability. The rows are parallel and are not translations.

mistakes: Reviewing the strands and skipping the third question about the mixing.
Letting a strong survey lend borrowed credibility to a thin qualitative strand.
Describing both methods in detail and none of the mixing.

recall.q: What are the three quality questions?
recall.a: Is the quantitative strand sound, is the qualitative strand sound, and is the mixing sound.

recall.q: Who is associated with legitimation?
recall.a: Onwuegbuzie and Johnson, with Tashakkori and Teddlie also pushing the field to formalise it.

recall.q: What does GRAMMS stand for?
recall.a: Good Reporting of A Mixed Methods Study.

recall.q: Which low-cost practice raises credibility and is rarely done?
recall.a: Taking findings back to participants.

recall.q: Which one thing to check in conclusions?
recall.a: Whether they could be written from one strand alone.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.big_idea: Four examples show the same pattern: **the value lives in the join**, and the key decision was taken months before it mattered.
in_plain_words: A cash-transfer trial with an embedded process strand explains heterogeneity and makes a null result interpretable. A health survey with deviant-case interviews explains three lagging blocks. An exploratory sequential study builds an empowerment scale from local accounts. A convergent study triangulates a leakage estimate from survey, records and interviews.

Real programmes have budgets and deadlines. RealWorld Evaluation argues mixing is often the practical answer, using secondary data in place of a baseline and a small second strand to interpret a thin one. Its discipline is to name what was given up, which is better than reporting as if nothing was.

key_terms.meaning: A qualitative strand on delivery and reception inside a trial.
Thinking aloud through a draft instrument to catch misreadings.
Welfare benefits that do not reach the intended households.
Bamberger's approach to evaluation under tight budgets and time.
Bars and interview reasons shown side by side.

worked_example.title: Triangulating leakage
worked_example.setup: Example 4 uses four sources, each biased in a different direction.
steps: Household survey self-report under-reports from fear of consequences.
Official records show what was recorded, by those involved.
Interviews with intermediaries carry their position in the transaction.
Where survey and records diverge, the interviews explain the gap.
Report a bounded range plus which source is likely to under- or overstate.
worked_example.answer: A bounded range with an account of each source's bias, in place of a single number.

mistakes: Adding a process strand after a disappointing result. It cannot recover what happened during the trial period.
Forgetting to retain an identifier at survey stage, which makes explanatory follow-up impossible.
Reporting a single number when sources with opposite biases cannot agree on magnitude.

recall.q: Why does an embedded process strand matter for a null result?
recall.a: It separates a wrong theory from a programme that never happened.

recall.q: What requirement is set at survey stage in Example 2?
recall.a: A retained identifier and consent to recontact.

recall.q: What explained the three low blocks in Example 2?
recall.a: Interviews attributed them to a closed sub-centre and night-time transport fears (illustrative).

recall.q: What does cognitive testing catch?
recall.a: More measurement error than later statistical adjustment.

recall.q: What do all four examples share?
recall.a: A purpose before a design, an early meeting point, a decision taken months before it mattered, and a claim neither strand makes alone.

sections.title: Common Pitfalls
sections.big_idea: Seven pitfalls recur. Most are **planning failures**, so each can be answered before any data is collected.
in_plain_words: The first three concern the work itself: parallel play with no integration, qualitative material used as decoration, and ignoring divergence. Test them bluntly: delete one strand and see whether the conclusions survive, ask what a quote would have to say to change the finding, and look for a disagreement paragraph.

The others are planning failures: priority that drifts to the survey, too little skill or time for the second strand, forcing a second method the question does not need, and a vague design that drifts. A pre-flight checklist and a one-line protocol entry address them before fieldwork starts.

children.label: Choice failure
items: Forcing methods the question does not need

key_terms.meaning: A quant chapter and a qual chapter that never speak.
Quotes that illustrate a number and change nothing.
Adding a method because 'mixed methods' sounds rigorous.
Design, priority and integration eroding mid-study.
Six checks answerable before data collection.

worked_example.title: The delete-one-strand test
worked_example.setup: Illustrative report with a survey chapter, an interview chapter and a discussion citing both.
steps: Cover the qualitative chapter.
Reread the conclusions.
If nothing becomes unsupported, the qualitative strand was never load-bearing.
Add a joint display and a statement of what the two together support.
worked_example.answer: If conclusions survive intact, you had parallel play and need a joint display and a meta-inference.

mistakes: Trusting the numbers when strands disagree and shelving the interviews.
Putting a qual analyst in no design meetings and then saying priority was equal.
Using 'and also' to attach a second strand the question does not need.

recall.q: What is the test for parallel play?
recall.a: Delete one strand; if conclusions survive intact, nothing was mixed.

recall.q: What symptoms show priority drifted to one strand?
recall.a: The other strand gets one paragraph, or sample sizes appear for one strand only.

recall.q: What is the honest test for forcing methods?
recall.a: Can you state a question that needs both?

recall.q: What should be recorded in the protocol about divergence?
recall.a: That it is an expected and reportable outcome.

recall.q: How many checks are in the pre-flight list?
recall.a: Six.

sections.title: Practice & Tools
sections.big_idea: Mixed work is team work. **Bring both specialists in at design**, choose tools that link the strands, and write the report so integration can be audited.
in_plain_words: Few researchers are equally strong in both traditions, so most strong work is a team. Both specialists are needed to frame the question, sample, design instruments and integrate. No software integrates for you: Dedoose, NVivo and ATLAS.ti record the join, and KoboToolbox plus R plus a shared spreadsheet joint display is a complete stack.

Structure the report with the design in notation up front, each strand on its own terms, a dedicated integration section and meta-inferences leading the discussion. Reviewers reject mixed papers for thin integration or a strand judged thin, so justify the mixing, show the join and use a reporting standard such as GRAMMS.

diagram.caption: a report that lets integration be audited

key_terms.meaning: Reporting checklist for mixed-methods studies.
Tool built for mixed-methods integration; links codes to variables.
Free, offline-capable collection of both data types.
Table arraying findings from both strands.
Makes the design legible; separate from a quality standard.

worked_example.title: Pre-empt reviewer objections
worked_example.setup: Four objections from the slide Publishing. Pair each with a defence.
steps: 'The strands are not integrated': a named integration section with joint displays.
'The qualitative sample is too small': state the sampling logic, information power and not representativeness.
'The survey is underpowered': report power for what the survey is actually claiming.
'Why mixed methods at all?': the one-sentence question that needs both strands.
worked_example.answer: Integration section, sampling logic, relevant power, and the one-sentence question.

mistakes: Bringing the qualitative specialist in at analysis, when the frame is fixed and no linking identifier exists.
Expecting software to produce the meta-inference.
Skipping a reader from each tradition when testing the draft.

recall.q: Which stages need both specialists?
recall.a: Framing the question, sampling design, instrument design and integration.

recall.q: What should a reader find in thirty seconds?
recall.a: Your meta-inference.

recall.q: What does GRAMMS do for reviewers?
recall.a: It makes your design legible to a reviewer from either tradition.

recall.q: Which text is written for constrained conditions?
recall.a: Bamberger et al., RealWorld Evaluation.

recall.q: Which resource suits MEL practitioners?
recall.a: BetterEvaluation.

notes.2: Use the agenda as a reading order: what mixing is, why, the worldview question, the four designs, choosing, sampling, integration, quality, examples, pitfalls and tools. **Integration is section 7 and the heart of the course**, so if time is short read sections 1, 4 and 7 first.
notes.4: Remember the test as one word: integration. A survey and some interviews in one project are **two studies in a trench coat**. Check yourself against the right-hand column: interviews chosen because of the survey, a finding neither strand reaches alone, and one design set before fieldwork.
notes.5: Run the four-question test on the last mixed-methods report you read. Most fail the third, the point where the strands met. The fourth is diagnostic: **a report where the strands agree on everything** has usually not looked hard, or dropped what did not fit. Ask where numbers and words actually talk.
notes.6: Read the table as three upgrades from a bare number to a usable claim. The third row is the classic case in evaluation: a null result could mean a wrong theory or **a programme never delivered**, and only implementation data separates them. Treat 'one plus one equals three' as a promise you must earn.
notes.7: Use the two lists as a matching exercise: pair each strength on one side with the weakness it covers on the other. Quantitative work gives scale and comparison, qualitative gives mechanism and surprise. **Mixing offsets blind spots**, so ask which blind spot your question has before you choose.
notes.8: Keep the history short in your head: a conflict over whether the two traditions could coexist, purposes mapped in 1989, then designs and a third methodological movement in the 2000s. The live disputes now concern **how to integrate well**. The philosophy still matters because it shapes how you treat the qualitative strand.
notes.9: Match each MEL question to the strand that answers it. 'Did it work?' needs numbers, while 'why here and not there?' needs mechanism. The cheapest addition is a **short process strand**, which stops you concluding a theory failed when the programme was never delivered. Scale-up needs effect size and conditions together.
notes.10: Say these cautions aloud in a planning meeting. Mixing multiplies skills, time and coordination, and **two weak strands do not make one strong study**. Adding interviews to a poor survey frame leaves the frame broken. Mix because the question demands it, and budget for integration time.
notes.11: The roadmap splits the course into foundations and practice. You will spend most effort on choosing, sampling and integrating. The slide also points to two companion courses, so **this course covers combining the strands**, and the others teach each strand on its own.
notes.13: Learn the five purposes in order with a mnemonic you invent: triangulation, complementarity, development, initiation, expansion. The instruction at the foot is the key one: **name your purpose before your design**. Each purpose implies a different design and a different meaning for agreement, as the next slides show.
notes.14: Test any claim of triangulation against four conditions: same construct, strong strands, independence, and a chance to disagree. The third is broken constantly, since **the same households through the same enumerator is one source**. If you cannot meet all four, call the purpose complementarity instead.
notes.15: Choose complementarity when the strands describe different facets, such as how many girls dropped out and what dropping out meant. Here **agreement is not expected**, so avoid the label triangulation. Naming it correctly stops a reader expecting corroboration that the design cannot deliver.
notes.16: Development is sequential, so strand B depends on what A finds. The qual-to-quan row is how good instruments get built in unfamiliar settings. Because the second strand cannot be costed precisely until the first reports, **plan a decision point** instead of a fixed second phase.
notes.17: Initiation is the purpose nobody plans, and the clinic example shows it: high satisfaction against private fury about waiting. **The contradiction is the discovery**, perhaps because satisfaction measured low expectations. Treat clashes as findings to investigate, and leave slack in the timeline to pursue them.
notes.18: Expansion gives each strand its own component, usually quant for outcomes and qual for process. It is legitimate, and it is the weakest form of mixing, because **nothing forces the strands to meet**. Name it plainly and add a deliberate integration step so it does not become parallel play.
notes.19: Use the two tables as a lookup before you write conclusions. The third column matters most: **only triangulation makes agreement meaningful**. In the other four purposes, saying the strands 'confirmed each other' claims more than the design supports. Good studies combine purposes, so say which strand serves which.
notes.20: Let the purpose choose the design. Triangulation points to concurrent collection, development to sequential, and initiation to any design with slack after first results. Complementarity can run convergent or embedded, and expansion runs in parallel with a deliberate integration point. **Choose the design after the purpose**, and write the reason down.
notes.22: A worldview is a set of beliefs about what exists and how we know it, and the strands often differ. The researcher's role causes most friction: closeness to participants is **contamination to one strand and access to the other**. You need not resolve this, but you must notice it, or it gets blamed on personalities.
notes.23: Read the table as two poles and avoid treating them as two camps. The last row has practical consequences: asking 'is it reliable?' of interviews or 'is it credible?' of a survey **imports the wrong standard**. Almost nobody holds either pole purely, so use it to spot where a disagreement comes from.
notes.24: This is the objection mixed methods had to answer: methods are tied to worldviews, so combining them is incoherent. Know its name, the **incompatibility thesis**, because the next two slides give the standard reply and a reviewer may still raise it.
notes.25: Pragmatism answers the objection by putting the question first. Use the three prompts in order: what is the question, what would answer it, what follows for action. Keep the critics' point in mind too: **'whatever works' hides a view of what counts as working**.
notes.26: Learn pragmatism through the right-hand column, the things critics say it claims: arbitrary method choice, truth as whatever is convenient, identical assumptions, and excuses for poor method. It claims none of them. Apply the slide's test: **can you say what would count as being wrong?**
notes.27: Four stances are on offer: purist, pragmatist, dialectical and equity-led. The dialectical stance deliberately holds paradigms in tension and mines the friction, which is **initiation as a philosophy**. The equity-led stance asks whose interests the study serves, so consider it when you work with marginalised groups.
notes.28: Use this slide on a team where each strand is staffed by people trained to see the other as sloppy or naive. Both traditions reduce error, use transparent procedures and accept that findings can be wrong. **Rigour belongs to no method**, and the last row is a shared test: could the evidence have contradicted the framing?
notes.29: State your stance in one sentence in the methods. Watch your own wording for the tell in the third row: calling a qualitative strand 'indicative' or **apologising for its sample size** applies a sampling logic it never claimed. Depth has no n. Expect disagreement and plan what you will do with it.
notes.31: Learn four marks: capitals for the dominant strand, lower case for the supporting one, a plus for concurrent and an arrow for sequential. Two decisions follow, **timing and priority**. Writing QUAN → qual commits you in a way that 'mixed methods' does not, so put the notation in your proposal.
notes.32: Read the diagram left to right: two strands run together, each collected and analysed on its own, then merged and compared at interpretation. It suits triangulation. The risk is the join, so **schedule the merge** and name who does it, and keep the strands independent until then.
notes.33: Remember the sequence: survey and results first, then follow-up interviews that explain surprises, outliers and group differences. It is the most common design in evaluation. **Protect the budget for phase two** before phase one begins, since the interviews are the whole point.
notes.34: Here qualitative work leads: explore, find themes, build an instrument or typology, then test it at scale. This matches the 'development' purpose. Plan for **phase one running long**, because that squeezes phase two, and keep the instrument tied to what respondents actually said.
notes.35: An embedded design nests a supportive strand inside a dominant one, classically a qualitative process evaluation inside a trial. It asks a **different but related question**. The risk is treating the embedded strand as decoration, so give it its own question and sampling, and a named link to the main analysis.
notes.36: Use the comparison to match a design to its failure. Each design's characteristic failure is a scheduling failure: convergent designs fail at the join, sequential ones at the **squeezed second phase**. Protect phase two's budget in advance, or the follow-up interviews become six rushed calls in the last week.
notes.37: The four designs are building blocks, and you may chain them across years. More phases mean more integration points, and each needs **a named person and a scheduled week**. Otherwise the strands stop talking without anyone noticing, which is the danger of complex designs.
notes.38: Read each notation with three rules: capitals mean priority, position means order, the connector means timing. Practise on the four rows, especially the second: a short survey used only to pick interviewees is a **legitimate sequential design**. Describe the survey as a sampling tool, since calling it a findings source overstates it.
notes.40: Start from the question and let it point to a design, using the table. The last row is the honest one: sometimes a **single strand done well** is the answer. Write the question as one sentence first; if it contains 'and why' or 'and how common', the conjunction chooses the design.
notes.41: Pick timing by what you need. Concurrent is faster and suits triangulation, but the strands cannot shape each other. Sequential lets A shape B, at the price of time. If a deadline forces concurrent, **say so instead of calling it a design choice**, and schedule a meeting between the teams.
notes.42: Priority is set by resourcing whether or not anyone decides it. A design declared equal with 80 per cent of the budget on the survey is a **QUAN(qual) design that has not admitted it**. Decide openly, write it in the notation, and if you cannot protect both budgets, choose which strand leads.
notes.43: Name the interface points in the proposal. The second row, **linked identifiers at data collection**, must be planned at the start, because without them the interesting integration becomes impossible. Compare the weak sentence on the slide with the specific joint display it offers, and write yours at that level.
notes.44: Use the chooser as a shortcut: find your aim, copy the notation into your proposal, and use the 'because' column when a reviewer asks why. Two entries are easy to miss: **quan → QUAL** for identifying whom to study in depth, and the dialectical stance for provoking new questions.
notes.45: List your constraints before choosing a design. A six-month timeline rules out a real phase two, and one researcher rules out concurrent strands. The common error is picking a design you cannot resource: it fails as **a second phase shrunk to six phone calls**. A smaller design done properly is better.
notes.46: Put six lines in the protocol: purpose, notation, priority and why, interface points, who integrates and when, and what happens if strands diverge. The last two separate **a design from an intention**. Record deviations as they happen, since an honest account of drift beats a tidy one.
notes.48: Hold both logics: quantitative sampling aims to represent a population, qualitative sampling to illuminate a phenomenon. Choosing interviewees at random from the survey satisfies one logic and defeats the other. In row four, **a bad quantitative sample is unrepresentative; a bad qualitative one is uninformative**.
notes.49: Choose sampling timing by your purpose. Concurrent samples preserve the independence triangulation needs, while sequential ones let you explain specific results. Decide **before the survey runs** whether individual-level linking is needed, since an identifier and consent for follow-up cannot be added afterwards.
notes.50: Nesting joins a person's numbers to their words, the tightest integration at case level. It has four requirements, and the fourth concerns integrity: **state selection criteria in advance**, or you risk choosing cases to confirm the story you already believe. Retained contact details are also a data-protection matter.
notes.51: Name your case-selection strategy in the methods. Extreme, typical, deviant, maximum-variation and confirming cases each answer a different question. The third row is the most productive: **cases the model predicted badly** are where an unmeasured factor is working. 'Twenty interviews' says little; the strategy says what the strand supports.
notes.52: Size each strand by its own logic: surveys by the precision needed for the smallest subgroup you report, interviews by saturation. 'Only 25 interviews?' is the wrong question for a strand that reached saturation. Remember the first row: **a survey powered for districts cannot be split later** by caste and gender.
notes.53: Compare the two frames in writing, including dates. The third row creates **false divergence**: two strands from different seasons will disagree about food, work and migration. When strands diverge, first check whether they described the same population at the same time. Sample qualitative cases from inside the survey sites.
notes.54: A representative survey can bury small groups, and purposive qualitative sampling is how you over-listen to them. The second row is where mixed designs help most: **go to the households that stopped coming**. Then write down who you could not reach, so no one mistakes your sample for the population.
notes.55: Write the one-page sampling plan before fieldwork. The fourth row, **how the two samples relate**, is unique to mixed methods and most often left implicit, and it decides whether integration is possible. Include who will be missed, stated now and not discovered later.
notes.57: Apply the removal test: take out either strand and see whether the conclusions barely change. If they do, you never integrated. Integration is scheduling as much as design, because it has no deliverable of its own. **Name a person and a week** or it gets absorbed by whatever is late.
notes.58: Match the way of integrating to the design you chose. Connecting happens almost automatically in sequential designs, embedding sits inside a larger design, and **merging is the hardest and most valuable**: someone must sit with both datasets and build the comparison. The joint display on the next slide is the tool.
notes.59: Build a joint display with a row per finding and a column per strand. The final column is the work: **writing what the row means jointly**. In the satisfaction row the strands diverge, which prompts a check of question wording. A display whose last column restates the other two has integrated nothing.
notes.60: Pick one striking finding and follow it into the other strand, then back again: survey gap, interview reasons, then a variable that tests them. Report the trail including where it went cold. Do it for **three or four findings only**. A reason heard repeatedly with no survey variable shows a gap in the instrument.
notes.61: Quantitising counts themes and qualitising builds profiles, and both lose something. The warning is in the first row: '12 of 20' invites reading **60 per cent as an estimate**. Add the slide's sentence saying counts are within a purposive sample and are not prevalence estimates, and keep the originals.
notes.62: Convergence is only as strong as the independence behind it. Report it explicitly, then say what would have counted as divergence. It is weak when respondents, visit and enumerator are shared, or when both instruments framed the question alike. The more surprising the agreement, **the more it counts**.
notes.63: Treat divergence as a finding. Work through the five checks in order: different things measured, different populations or periods, social desirability, one strand wrong, both right. The satisfaction case is typical: **a stranger with a form** in a public space gets the safe answer. Report which explanation you settled on.
notes.64: Write the meta-inference as its own subsection, labelled as drawing on both strands. Use the test on the slide: if the conclusions could come from one strand alone, **the mixing produced nothing**. A conclusion across both strands qualifies, and a summary of each in turn does not.
notes.66: Remember three bars: the quantitative strand on its own terms, the qualitative strand on its own terms, and the quality of the mixing. Reviewers skip the third, yet **it decides whether the study was mixed at all**. Together the three make the standard higher than for a single-method study.
notes.67: Use the parallel terms as a translator, remembering the rows are parallel and are not equivalents. Transferability puts judgement with the reader, so a qualitative report owes **thick context** in place of a confidence interval. The under-supplied item is the audit trail: how codes were derived, who coded and how disagreements were settled.
notes.68: Legitimation names the question the two traditions have no word for: is the join sound? Run the four questions over your own draft. **The fourth, was divergence handled, is the one most reports fail**, and fixing it usually means adding the paragraph you were tempted to leave out.
notes.69: The slide lists five threats: sample integration, sequential, conversion, weakness minimisation and paradigmatic. Use them as a checklist. Two deserve attention. Weakness minimisation lets a **strong survey lend borrowed credibility** to a thin qualitative strand, and sequential error carries phase one's problems into phase two. Add a decision point between the phases.
notes.70: Check design quality and interpretive rigour separately, because they fail independently. Then do the practical test on the slide: **mark every conclusion against its supporting strand**. Anything unmarked is either a meta-inference to label or an assertion to remove.
notes.71: Pick practices from the table that cost little: pre-specify the design, build a joint display, report divergence, and have each strand read the other's draft. The fourth is nearly free and effective, since each reader catches the other's over-claims. **Return findings to participants**; it is rarely budgeted.
notes.72: Report the mixing as well as the methods, using five items: purpose, design in notation, where the strands met, what diverged and what each strand could not support. Most reports describe both methods and none of the mixing. These are **five sentences in the methods section** that make the study assessable.
notes.73: If you can check only one thing, use the table: a named integration point in a proposal, a joint display in a draft, and in the conclusions whether they **could be written from one strand alone**. Judge the join as well as the parts. The join is the part nobody owns.
notes.75: Use the RCT with an embedded process evaluation as your model for QUAN(qual). The embedded strand makes a null result interpretable: no effect could mean a wrong theory or **a programme that never happened**, and the two call for opposite decisions. Embed it from the start.
notes.76: See what the qualitative strand establishes that a trial cannot: delivery, what participants understood, what else changed, and why some sites did better. The meta-inference, that the effect ran through women's control of the cash, **needed both strands**. The fourth row is where the scale-up decision is made.
notes.77: This is the explanatory sequential template: a survey finds three lagging blocks, and deviant-case interviews explain them. Notice the last row, a requirement set months earlier: **a retained identifier and consent to recontact**. Decide those at survey stage, before anyone knows what needs explaining.
notes.78: Read the chart and the interview findings together. The bars show which three blocks lag, and the interviews give the reason: a closed sub-centre and night-time transport fears. That reason is the meta-inference **the bars alone could not give**. Remember that the data are illustrative.
notes.79: Follow the four phases from local accounts to a validated scale: domains and language from interviews, draft items in respondents' words, cognitive testing, then administration at scale. Cognitive testing is skipped most often and costs least. **Thinking aloud through a draft with ten respondents** catches measurement error that statistics cannot.
notes.80: Triangulation works here because each source is biased in a different direction: survey self-report under-reports, records reflect those involved, interviews reflect position, and observation has observer effects. Contrast it with the same-respondent case on slide 62. **Expect divergence**, and report a bounded range plus which source likely understates or overstates.
notes.81: RealWorld Evaluation accepts that budgets and timelines are tight. Use the constraint table as a menu of honest responses, such as embedding a small second strand when you can fund only one. The key practice is making compromises explicit: **name what was given up**. Fifteen good embedded interviews beat none.
notes.82: Before designing, write the meta-inference you hope to reach, then check that both strands are needed to get there. The four examples share a pattern in the third row: **a decision made months earlier** (identifier, embedded strand, selection rule) that could not be added later at any price.
notes.84: Apply the delete-one-strand test to your own report: cover the qualitative chapter and reread the conclusions. If nothing becomes unsupported, you had parallel play. The cause is often a writing failure, with **integration done in the analyst's head** and never put on the page. The reader cannot check what they cannot see.
notes.85: Test every quote by asking what it would have to say for you to change the finding. If no quote could have changed it, **the qualitative data served as illustration**. Quotes that explain a district difference or challenge the measure do analytic work. Decorative quotes mean fieldwork was paid for and then went unused.
notes.86: Priority should be a decision. Use the symptom table to diagnose accidental weighting: one paragraph for a strand that cost a third of the budget, sample sizes for only one strand, **a qualitative analyst absent from design meetings**. Write priority into the protocol in notation. Unequal weighting is fine when chosen.
notes.87: Plan both costs up front: two field rounds with an analysis gap between them, analysts from both traditions working in overlap, and **weeks for integration**. A team strong in one tradition produces a token second strand, because the weak side cannot tell thin data from sufficient data.
notes.88: Run the honest test: can you state a question that needs both strands? The table gives four examples, and two of them need only one method. Write the question in a sentence. If it needs an **'and also' to bring in the second strand**, that strand is probably decoration. Defend a single strong method openly.
notes.89: Divergence is the finding most likely to be right and least likely to be published. Use the table to turn bad responses into good ones, such as checking who the administrative denominator excludes. Be suspicious of **suspiciously good agreement**: two strands sharing a frame are one measurement reported twice.
notes.90: Write one line in the protocol before collecting data: design in notation, sampling rule and integration method, like the example on the slide. Drift is invisible from inside, because **each shortcut looks reasonable** under time pressure. The pre-specified line is what lets you notice you took them.
notes.91: Use the pre-flight checklist before any fieldwork, because each item gets costlier to fix once data collection starts. Five of the six checks are integration questions asked early enough to act on. If one fails, **fix the design now**, and answer the divergence question in the protocol.
notes.93: Bring both specialists into the design stage. The common failure is inviting the qualitative specialist at analysis, when the frame is fixed and **the linking identifier was never collected**. Treat respect for each other's craft as a working requirement, since contempt held privately resolves every divergence in one direction.
notes.94: Choose tools by what you must join. Dedoose links codes to variables, NVivo and ATLAS.ti code qualitative data, and R, Stata and Kobo cover the quantitative side. Use the checks on the right before committing. **No software integrates for you**; what a code and a variable mean together stays with the analyst.
notes.95: Structure the report so integration can be audited: design and rationale in notation up front, each strand on its own terms, a dedicated integration section with joint displays, then meta-inferences first in the discussion. **A reader should find your meta-inference in thirty seconds.** Test the draft on a reader from each tradition.
notes.96: Pre-empt the four typical reviewer objections using the right-hand column. Two come from a reviewer applying one tradition's standards to the other strand, so **name the standard you are applying**. GRAMMS makes your design legible to either reader. It is a reporting standard, and quality is a separate matter.
notes.97: Choose by need. Start with Creswell and Plano Clark if you must design a study this quarter, and with Greene if you must justify why you are mixing. Tashakkori and Teddlie cover legitimation and inference quality. **Bamberger is written for the conditions most readers face**: incomplete baselines and short timelines.
notes.98: Pick resources by the right-hand column. Read published joint displays before building your own, because the format varies and good ones show what a display must make visible. Pair this deck with Qualitative Methods 101 for the strand most readers are weaker on, and with Theory of Change for the integration point.
notes.99: Use these five lines as a revision card. The fifth sums it up: **one plus one equals three only when the strands actually meet**. Before you close the deck, restate each line in terms of your own study, naming where yours will meet and what you will do if the strands disagree.
